ety.text: From Middle English up, op, oup, from Old English upp, up, ūp (“up”), from Proto-West Germanic *upp, *ūp, from Proto-Germanic *upp, *eup (“up”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian ap (“up”), West Frisian op (“up”), Dutch op (“up”), German Low German up, op (“up”), German auf (“up”), Danish op (“up”), Swedish upp (“up”), Icelandic upp (“up”), Gothic 𐌹𐌿𐍀 (iup, “up”).

senses.d: Away from the surface of the Earth or other planet; in opposite direction to the downward pull of gravity.
ex: I looked up and saw the airplane overhead.
Shoots grow up and roots grow down.

senses.d: To or at a physically higher or more elevated position.
ex: All day we climbed up and up.
Lift the carpet up and look underneath.

senses.d: To an upright or erect position.
ex: sit up; stand up; get up out of bed

senses.d: To a higher level of some quantity or notional quantity, such as price, volume, pitch, happiness, etc.
ex: Gold has gone up with the uncertainty in the world markets.
Turn it up, I can barely hear it.

senses.d: To or towards what is considered the top of something, irrespective of whether this is presently physically higher.
ex: Go back up to the top of the page.
As I lay on my back, a pain shot up from my toes to my chest.

senses.d: To the north (as north is at the top of typical maps).
ex: I live in Florida, but I'm going up to New York to visit my family this weekend.

senses.d: Towards or at a central place, or any place that is visualised as ‘up’ by virtue of local features or local convention, or arbitrarily, irrespective of direction or elevation change.
ex: We travelled from Yorkshire up to London.
I'm going up to the other end of town.

senses.d: Towards the principal terminus, towards milepost zero.
To university, especially to Cambridge or Oxford.
ex: She's going up to read Classics this September.
A precocious mathematician, Babbage was already well versed in the Continental mathematical notations when he went up to Cambridge.

senses.d: Against the wind or current.
Toward the top of.
ex: The cat climbed up the tree.
They walk up the steps.

senses.d: Toward the center, source, or main point of reference; toward the end at which something is attached.
ex: The information made its way up the chain of command to the general.
I felt something crawling up my arm.

senses.d: From south to north of.
ex: We sailed up the East Coast of England from Ipswich to South Shields.
Though the storm raged up the East Coast, it has become increasingly apparent that New Jersey took the brunt of it.

senses.d: Further along (in any direction).
ex: Go up the street until you see the sign.

senses.d: From the mouth towards the source of (a river or waterway).
ex: He led an expedition up the Amazon.

senses.d: Of a person: having sex with.
ex: Phwoar, look at that bird. I'd love to be up her.

senses.d: At (a given place, especially one imagined to be higher or more distant from a central location).
ex: I'll see you later up the snooker club.
“I'll tell you how I got on in the fight if I should see you up the Smokers.”

senses.d: Facing upwards.
ex: Turn the cloth over so that the patterned side is up.

senses.d: On or at a physically higher level.
ex: The flood waters are up again across large areas of the country.

senses.d: Headed or designated to go upward (as an escalator, stairway, elevator etc.) or toward (as a run-up).
ex: Where is the up escalator?

senses.d: Fitted or fixed at a high or relatively high position, especially on a wall or ceiling.
ex: All the notices are up now.
The Christmas decorations are up.

senses.d: Available to view or use; made public; posted.
ex: Is your new video up yet? I looked on the website, but I couldn't find it.

senses.d: Aloft.
ex: The kite is up!

senses.d: Raised; lifted.
ex: The castle drawbridge was up.
Don't go into the living room just now – I've got the carpet up.

senses.d: Of a river, in flood or at a high level.
ex: In the late afternoon we rode among the fine trees of the Barker, which was ‘up’ too, but not so strongly as the Lennard.

senses.d: Built, constructed.
ex: Are the new buildings up yet?

senses.d: Standing; upright.
ex: The audience were up and on their feet.

senses.d: The direction opposed to the pull of gravity.
ex: Up is a good way to go.

senses.d: A positive thing, or a time or situation when things are going well.
ex: I hate almost everything about my job. The only up is that it's so close to home.
There are many ups to caravanning, but also many downs.

senses.d: An up quark.
An upstairs room of a two story house.
ex: She lives in a two-up two-down.

senses.d: To physically raise or lift.
ex: We upped anchor and sailed away.

senses.d: To increase the level or amount of.
ex: If we up the volume, we may be able to hear what he says.
As usual, they've upped the prices for Valentine's Day.

senses.d: To promote.
ex: It wasn’t long before they upped him to Vice President.
The other day Mr. Meyer came to see me in Weinbergers, it caused a great sensation & I think upped me a lot in prestige there

senses.d: To rise to a standing position; hence, by extension, to act suddenly; see also up and.
ex: She was sitting there quietly, then all of a sudden she upped and left.
He just upped and quit.

senses.d: To ascend; to climb up.
ex: "Will ye up, lass, and ride behind me?".

senses.d: To upload.
ex: 100 new apps and games have just been upped.

Inherited from Middle French hault, from Old French haut, halt (“high, tall, elevated”), a conflation of Frankish *hauh, *hōh (“high, tall, elevated”) and Latin altus (“high, raised, profound”). Akin to Old High German hōh (“high, tall, elevated”). More at high, haughty.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin augmentāre, from Latin augmentum (“growth, increase”), from augeō (“increase”). Cognate of English augment.
